column2: Tall thin woman with lens dislocation (Marfan), wide pulse pressure and early diastolic decrescendo murmur: aortic regurgitation from root dilatation.
Fever with prominent v waves and a pansystolic murmur louder on inspiration is tricuspid regurgitation, likely right-sided endocarditis.
Exertional dizziness with a brisk carotid upstroke, S4 and crescendo–decrescendo murmur at the lower left sternal border is HCM; AS has a slow-rising pulse.
Symptomatic sinus bradycardia with hypotension in inferior STEMI: IV atropine 500 µg (to 3 mg) first; pacing or isoprenaline if it fails; reperfuse.
Asymptomatic ectopics and short NSVT with stable haemodynamics: observe, continue beta-blocker and correct K/Mg. Prophylactic antiarrhythmics do not help.
Accelerated idioventricular rhythm (60–120/min) after reperfusion is benign and self-limiting: observe.
Radiofemoral delay with weak femorals and arm hypertension is the hallmark of coarctation; rib notching on CXR.
Bounding pulse, warm peripheries, flap and drowsiness in COPD reflect acute CO2 retention: ABG, target SpO2 88–92%, NIV if acidotic.
Collapsing pulse, wide pulse pressure and pistol-shot femorals (Traube) indicate severe aortic regurgitation.
Pulsus paradoxus, hypotension, raised JVP with absent y descent and muffled sounds is tamponade; Kussmaul sign and knock suggest constriction.
Ejection click with an aortic-area ejection murmur in a young adult suggests bicuspid aortic valve; a soft A2 means significant stenosis.
Soft pulmonary flow murmur with fixed S2 splitting is ASD; the murmur is from increased flow across the pulmonary valve.
Systolic murmur loudest between the scapulae with arm hypertension is coarctation; check radiofemoral delay.
Harsh ejection murmur with thrill in the left 2nd space and a soft delayed P2 is congenital pulmonary stenosis; balloon valvuloplasty.
Double right heart border, prominent LA appendage and elevated left main bronchus mean left atrial enlargement, classically mitral stenosis.
Upper-lobe diversion, Kerley B lines, bat-wing shadowing and cardiomegaly are the CXR signs of left heart failure.
Trachea pulled right with elevated horizontal fissure and right hilum is right upper lobe collapse; bronchoscopy to exclude carcinoma.
Bilateral subpleural lower-zone reticulation with small lungs is IPF (UIP pattern); HRCT shows honeycombing.
A cavity with an air–fluid level after an alcohol binge is a lung abscess from aspiration (anaerobes, S. aureus).
Tapping apex, loud S1 and apical mid-diastolic rumble (left lateral, expiration) is mitral stenosis.
Heaving undisplaced apex, absent A2 and ejection murmur to the carotids indicate severe calcific aortic stenosis.
Pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge louder on inspiration with a pulsatile liver is tricuspid regurgitation.
Displaced volume-loaded apex, soft S1 and apical pansystolic murmur to the axilla is chronic mitral regurgitation.
Harsh pansystolic murmur with thrill at the lower left sternal edge, not varying with respiration and with a normal JVP, is a VSD.
A raised non-pulsatile JVP means obstruction above the RA: superior vena cava obstruction (lung cancer, lymphoma).
Giant systolic v waves occur when the RV ejects back through an incompetent tricuspid valve: tricuspid regurgitation.
Large a waves with a slow y descent and ascites indicate tricuspid stenosis, usually rheumatic with mitral stenosis.
Cannon a waves (atrium contracting against a closed tricuspid valve) indicate AV dissociation, typically complete heart block.
A JVP rising on inspiration (Kussmaul sign) is classic of constrictive pericarditis.
Sinus tachycardia is the commonest ECG finding in PE; S1Q3T3 reflects RV strain but is insensitive. Use Wells, D-dimer and CTPA.
RSR' in V1 with T inversion V1–V3, broad S in I and V6 and QRS ≥ 120 ms is right bundle-branch block.
Hypokalaemia: long PR, ST depression, flat T waves and prominent U waves.
Broad bifid P mitrale in II with a deep negative terminal P in V1 indicates left atrial enlargement, classically mitral stenosis.
ST elevation in II, III and aVF is inferior MI (usually RCA): primary PCI and check V4R for RV infarction.
Tall tented T waves are the earliest sign of hyperkalaemia (ACEi + spironolactone); check K⁺ and give IV calcium if ECG changes.
PEA after blunt chest trauma with distended neck veins, central trachea and equal breath sounds is tamponade: immediate pericardiocentesis.
Irregularly irregular narrow complexes without P waves is atrial fibrillation, often triggered by acute illness such as pneumonia.
Broad QRS with M-shaped R in V5–V6 and lateral T inversion is LBBB; cardiac sarcoid infiltrates the conducting system.
T-wave inversion in V1 (often V2–V3) is a normal juvenile pattern in children.
Digoxin slows AF rate without negative inotropy, suiting heart failure (with a beta-blocker). Avoid verapamil and diltiazem.
Metolazone (thiazide-like) acts synergistically with loop diuretics in resistant oedema; monitor K⁺, Na⁺ and renal function closely.
Spironolactone reduces HFrEF mortality (RALES) added to an ACE inhibitor; a beta-blocker is avoided here because of asthma.
Acute pulmonary oedema: sit up, oxygen if hypoxaemic, IV furosemide and nitrates if SBP > 110; routine opiates are no longer advised.
Oral furosemide relieves congestion but not mortality; use the lowest effective dose while prognostic therapy is optimised.
Inferior STEMI < 12 h: aspirin, P2Y12 loading and primary PCI within 120 min; fibrinolysis only if PCI is not available in time.
VF: immediate shock and CPR; adrenaline 1 mg and amiodarone 300 mg after the third shock.
Collapse with breathlessness and pleuritic pain after a flight is PE: oxygen, therapeutic anticoagulation and fluids; thrombolyse if unstable.
Malignant hypertension (papilloedema, haemorrhages) from glomerulonephritis: IV labetalol in a monitored bed, lowering MAP ≤ 25%. Avoid sublingual nifedipine.
Symptomatic sinus bradycardia: IV atropine 500 µg, repeated to 3 mg; then isoprenaline/adrenaline or transcutaneous pacing.
Clinic BP < 140/90 is not hypertension: lifestyle advice and periodic re-measurement.
A clinic reading of 140/90–179/119 must be confirmed by ABPM (or HBPM) before diagnosis (NICE NG136); then treat promptly given his diabetes.
Confirmed persistent hypertension despite lifestyle change needs drug treatment started in primary care; admission is unnecessary.
BP 220/120 without acute organ damage is hypertensive urgency: start oral treatment and review early; rapid lowering is dangerous.
BP 240/140 with papilloedema, haemorrhages and confusion is a hypertensive emergency: HDU, arterial line, IV labetalol/nitroprusside.
A normal NT-proBNP (< 400 ng/L non-acute) makes heart failure very unlikely; above 2000 ng/L, echo within 2 weeks.
Transthoracic Doppler echo confirms heart failure and its type (EF), valve disease and wall motion.
An ACE inhibitor with a beta-blocker is first line in HFrEF, reducing mortality and reversing remodelling; ARB if intolerant.
Loop diuretics are first-line for fluid overload in heart failure; thiazides are add-on for resistance.
Still symptomatic on ACEi and beta-blocker: add spironolactone (RALES ~30% mortality reduction) and an SGLT2 inhibitor; check K⁺.
Diarrhoea and vomiting cause hypokalaemia: weakness, cramps and prominent U waves. Replace K⁺ and check magnesium.
